headline: Semiconductors Hold the Line as Sellers Take the Rest
body_html:
Tuesday's session closed on a cautious note, with 309 stocks in our universe finishing lower against 233 that managed gains — a lopsided outcome that left most sectors nursing modest losses. The lone pocket of genuine strength was semiconductors, which edged up 1.04% as chip-equipment names led the charge. Applied Materials rose 5.26% and Onto Innovation added 5.21%, suggesting investors are still willing to pay up for exposure to the equipment layer of the semiconductor supply chain even as broader risk appetite cools heading into quarter-end.

The sector rotation told a clear story: money rotated away from materials, off 0.82%, and energy, which shed 0.91%, while software slipped 0.45%. Consumer and homebuilders each dipped fractionally, and healthcare was nearly flat at minus 0.09%. The defensive tilt across most of the tape points to lingering caution around geopolitical headlines — renewed U.S.-Iran diplomatic talks kept Gulf markets on edge, while fresh American sanctions targeting alleged weapons procurement for Tehran added another layer of uncertainty to energy sentiment.

The session's undisputed standout was Bloom Energy, which surged 10.77% — a striking move that ran counter to the broader energy sector's decline and underscored how idiosyncratic catalysts can cut through macro headwinds. STAAR Surgical's 7.47% jump provided a rare bright spot in an otherwise directionless healthcare tape. With September drawing to a close, Tuesday's price action suggests portfolio managers are in no hurry to add risk before the calendar turns.

briefs.headline: Fair Isaac Suffers a Brutal Quarter-End Blow
briefs.body: Fair Isaac shed 27.2% on Tuesday, making it by far the most punishing decliner across our entire universe. The financial-data firm's collapse dragged on sentiment in the broader financial-data space and served as a stark reminder that even well-regarded analytics businesses are not immune to sharp reassessments. No other stock in our universe came close to that level of damage.

briefs.headline: Coal Names Take a Double Hit as Materials Sector Slides
briefs.body: Alpha Metallurgical Resources fell 5.05% and Warrior Met Coal dropped 3.73%, with both metallurgical-coal producers contributing to the materials sector's 0.82% decline — the second-worst sector performance of the day. The twin selloff reflects continued pressure on industrial-commodity names as global demand signals remain mixed heading into the fourth quarter.

briefs.headline: Corning Bucks the Materials Gloom with a Solid Advance
briefs.body: While the broader materials sector finished near the bottom of Tuesday's leaderboard, Corning bucked the trend with a 5.04% gain, landing among the day's top six advancers. The glass-and-specialty-materials maker's move stood out as a rare exception within a sector that otherwise struggled, hinting at company-specific momentum rather than any broad materials recovery.

briefs.headline: Prediction Markets See a Stronger-Than-Expected Payrolls Print Ahead
briefs.body: Traders on prediction markets are wagering that September's U.S. jobs report will come in ahead of the consensus economist estimate — a view that, if correct, could complicate the Federal Reserve's rate calculus. The positioning adds a layer of event risk to an already cautious tape as investors prepare for Friday's data release.

briefs.headline: SPR Release Adds Supply Pressure to an Already Soft Energy Tape
briefs.body: The U.S. government announced plans to loan up to 40 million barrels of crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve under a previously arranged global agreement. The news landed as energy was already the worst-performing sector on Tuesday, down 0.91%, and oil-services name Innovex International declined 4.76%, suggesting the market is pricing in a less supportive near-term supply backdrop.

briefs.headline: Raimondo Flags Near-Term AI Job Displacement as the Real Risk
briefs.body: Former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo acknowledged that artificial intelligence will likely generate employment over the long run but warned that the immediate wave of AI-driven layoffs is the more pressing concern for workers and policymakers. Her comments echo a growing debate on Capitol Hill and in corporate boardrooms about the uneven short-term costs of rapid automation adoption.
